concept.name: Disposition effect
concept.definition: The empirically documented tendency of investors to sell winning positions too early and hold losing positions too long, named by Shefrin and Statman (1985) and confirmed in brokerage-account data by Odean (1998). It is a descriptive behavioral pattern, explained in part by prospect theory, mental accounting, and regret avoidance.
concept.intuition: Traders cash in winners quickly to enjoy the win, but let losers run because selling would mean admitting a mistake.
concept.mechanics: Odean measured it as the gap between the proportion of gains realized (PGR) and the proportion of losses realized (PLR) in account data; PGR exceeded PLR in all months except December, when tax-loss selling reverses it. Prospect theory supplies the mechanism: risk seeking in the loss domain (ride losers) and risk aversion in the gain domain (sell winners).
concept.formula: PGR = Realized Gains / (Realized Gains + Paper Gains); PLR = Realized Losses / (Realized Losses + Paper Losses); disposition effect present when PGR - PLR > 0 (Odean 1998).
concept.failure_modes: The effect weakens or reverses with tax-loss selling, in panics (high volatility), and among some professional groups; belief-driven trading can mimic or mask the preference-based effect. It is a population tendency, not a rule about any individual position.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a claim that holding losers is always wrong - rebalancing, mean reversion, or tax logic can justify it - nor that prospect theory alone explains it; belief revisions also contribute. It also does not imply winners should never be sold.
concept.example: In Odean's sample of 10,000 discount-brokerage accounts, a stock trading above its purchase price was about 1.5 times as likely to be sold as one trading below it, and the winners sold went on to outperform the losers kept.
